title: Childhood neurological symptoms revisited after adult seizures and cognitive difficulty
purpose: Separate childhood difficulties from later seizures and reported cognitive change.
decision_point: A researcher-designed pre-confirmation review during the admission at age 24. The age-based history, adult examination, EEG and structural imaging are requestable; biopsy, genetics and subsequent treatment are excluded. The report does not provide exact dates or a complete sequence within that admission.
opening: A 24-year-old woman is admitted for recurrent episodes of impaired consciousness preceded by headache and blurred vision. She has substantial cognitive difficulty, so obtain the longitudinal history from a caregiver and objective findings from records.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Reconstruct the age-based course, integrate seizures with childhood learning history and reported adult cognitive change, and provide a provisional differential and next assessment. After up to six question turns, give a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. A precise inherited diagnosis or variant is not required. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Published clinical facts and documented family observations are paraphrased into caregiver/record replies; no fluent first-person patient history is fabricated. The caregiver voice, pre-confirmation review, opening, six-turn task, requirements and release rules are researcher-designed. Requestable imaging and examination may already have been available to the real team; experimental withholding until requested does not change their chronology. No exact order or dates within the adult admission are invented. Biopsy/genetic confirmation and treatment outcomes are excluded. The report's caveat about unquantified adult cognitive progression is retained.
hidden: Biopsy findings, compound heterozygous SNORD118 variants and their classifications, the final disease label, lacosamide initiation and response, discussion/declining of bevacizumab and three-month follow-up. No functional study of the novel variant was performed; a biological effect is not an experimentally established fact.

facts.text: The first recorded symptoms were brief headache and visual-disturbance episodes at about age six, lasting several minutes.
Learning difficulties appeared at about seven, with persistently poor primary-school performance. Between ages 15 and 21, no substantial neurological deterioration was reported.

At age 22 she had a probable focal seizure progressing to a bilateral tonic-clonic event while cycling, preceded by headache and blurred vision, with incontinence and foaming at the mouth. From 22 to 24, episodes recurred once or twice monthly.

The family noticed further memory and everyday cognitive difficulty in early adulthood, especially after recurrent seizures began. This is a reported change on top of longstanding learning difficulty; the report has no serial standardized cognitive assessments to quantify that change.

The parents were reported to be clinically healthy and were not consanguineous. Her younger brother reported mild memory difficulty but remained functionally independent; he had not undergone the genetic testing described in the report.
At admission, muscle strength, sensation and gait were normal, and the ophthalmological examination was unremarkable. MMSE was 12. Formal neuropsychological testing beyond MMSE was not completed.
The admission EEG showed sharp and slow waves in the bilateral occipital and parietal regions.

At age six, CT had shown small intracranial calcifications. At the adult admission, CT showed widespread basal-ganglia and cerebellar calcifications and two cystic lesions with fluid levels. MRI showed right thalamic and parietal cysts plus diffuse periventricular/deep-white-matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.

reference: Preserve the distinction between childhood learning difficulty, a reported relatively stable adolescent interval, adult seizure onset and family-reported further cognitive deterioration. MMSE 12 establishes a low current score but does not quantify an acquired decline from childhood. Integrate received imaging and EEG with the clinical course to form a provisional structural, vascular, metabolic or inherited-neurological differential, with appropriate seizure assessment. Do not require the undisclosed biopsy, genetic result or final label. A healthy parental history does not settle inheritance, and the brother's symptoms do not establish the same condition. Requesting more detailed baseline/serial neuropsychological evidence is appropriate even though it is unavailable. Candidate essential requests and clinical prioritisation await confirmation.

answer:
**Clinical Problem**

A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures (1–2/month since age 22), longstanding learning difficulty from approximately age 7, and reported adult cognitive decline (MMSE 12). Structural imaging shows progressive intracranial calcifications—small at age 6, widespread in basal ganglia and cerebellum at 24—plus right thalamic and parietal cysts and diffuse periventricular/deep-white-matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity without enhancement or diffusion restriction. EEG shows bilateral occipital and parietal sharp and slow waves.

**Provisional Differential**

1. Genetic calcifying encephalopathy (e.g., primary familial brain calcification or related inherited syndrome): most consistent with progressive bilateral calcifications, cystic lesions, white-matter changes, childhood cognitive impairment, seizures, and a brother with mild memory difficulty. Uncertainty: no genetic or metabolic results are available in this packet.
2. Mitochondrial or metabolic encephalopathy: could explain calcifications, white-matter signal change, seizures, and cognitive decline. Uncertainty: no biochemical screening data supplied.
3. Vascular or structural calcification syndrome (e.g., Sturge-Weber spectrum): supported by calcifications and cystic changes, though absence of enhancement and the distribution are less typical.

**Next Assessment**

Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone; formal neuropsychological testing; targeted genetic panel or whole-exome sequencing; and consideration of prolonged EEG monitoring to characterise seizure semiology.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: All factual claims in the submission are grounded in the supplied evidence: seizure onset at 22 with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic progression and 1-2 monthly recurrences (Q1), learning difficulty from about age 7 (Q1), MMSE 12 and normal motor/sensory/gait/ophthalmological exam (Q4), bilateral occipito-parietal sharp and slow waves on EEG (Q2), childhood calcifications at age 6 and adult basal-ganglia/cerebellar calcifications with right thalamic/parietal cysts and T2/FLAIR white-matter change without restriction or enhancement (Q2), and the brother's mild memory difficulty with healthy non-consanguineous parents (Q3). No doses, values, or findings were invented. The differential is appropriately hedged: each of the three candidate explanations carries an explicit uncertainty statement (no genetic/metabolic results, no biochemical screening, atypical features for Sturge-Weber), consistent with the reference points not to overstate inheritance or undisclosed results. The only mild stretch is calling the calcifications 'progressive' based on two time points, but this is a reasonable reading of the supplied age-6 versus adult imaging and is not misleading. The response explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or unavailable, matching the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The submission synthesises the actually supplied evidence into a focused, clinically meaningful representation: recurrent focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures from age 22, learning difficulty from age 7 with reported adult cognitive decline (MMSE 12), progressive intracranial calcifications (age-6 CT vs adult CT/MRI), thalamic/parietal cysts, white-matter T2/FLAIR change, and bilateral occipito-parietal sharp and slow waves on EEG. It prioritises a genetic calcifying encephalopathy as the leading hypothesis, appropriately uses the brother's mild memory difficulty without overstating family history, and qualifies each hypothesis with the actual absence of genetic/metabolic data (Q2, Q3 feedback). It does not invent findings: it does not claim untreated status, normal milestones, or negative metabolic screens, and it correctly frames semiology of recurrent events as focal-to-bilateral based on the documented first event. The Sturge-Weber suggestion is a weaker, explicitly qualified third hypothesis rather than an unjustified commitment. Unresolved gaps (no genetic/biochemical results, no serial cognitive testing, uncharacterised recurrent-event semiology) are acknowledged, and next actions are proportionate. Minor limitations (e.g., not explicitly flagging that metabolic testing status is unknown rather than unperformed) do not alter the clinical framing. This meets the score-5 anchor: discriminating features highlighted, hypothesis generation guided, and material unresolved gaps made clear.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission gives a breadth-appropriate, prioritised differential grounded in the evidence actually supplied: progressive intracranial calcifications (age-6 CT vs adult CT), thalamic/parietal cysts, diffuse white-matter T2/FLAIR change without restriction or enhancement, bilateral occipito-parietal sharp-and-slow waves, childhood learning difficulty from age 7, seizure onset at 22, and MMSE 12. The top choice (genetic calcifying encephalopathy/primary familial brain calcification) is well supported and appropriately hedged given that genetics and metabolic screens are withheld (Q3 feedback). Mitochondrial/metabolic encephalopathy is a relevant alternative, and Sturge-Weber spectrum is a plausible structural-mimic consideration, with the noted atypical features. However, it falls short of a 5: discriminating findings are only partially explicit, a key dangerous and treatable mimic—hypoparathyroidism or other calcium/PTH disturbance—is raised only as a next test rather than included as a differential item, and Sturge-Weber is weakly supported (no port-wine stain or enhancement noted). Prioritisation is sensible and no case-critical diagnosis is missed, so this is a solid Score 4 rather than 3 or 5.

scores.name: Chronological precision
scores.reason: The submission presents events in correct chronological order with explicit temporal anchors: learning difficulty 'from approximately age 7', calcifications 'small at age 6, widespread... at 24', seizure onset at 'age 22' with recurrence '1–2/month since age 22', and current admission findings (MMSE 12, EEG, imaging) placed at presentation. No events are out of sequence and no sequencing errors are apparent, matching the Score 5 anchor for correct chronology with explicit temporal anchors.

scores.name: Trajectory interpretation
scores.reason: The submission correctly reconstructs the trajectory across the supplied evidence: childhood learning difficulty from about age 7 (Q1), a relatively stable adolescent interval, seizure onset at 22 with monthly recurrence (Q1), family-reported adult cognitive decline with MMSE 12 (Q4), and imaging evolution from small calcifications at age 6 to widespread basal-ganglia/cerebellar calcifications, cysts, and white-matter change at 24 (Q2), with bilateral occipito-parietal sharp/slow waves on EEG. The differential is graded (inherited calcifying encephalopathy first, supported by the imaging progression, cognitive course, and the brother's memory difficulty, with explicit uncertainty about absent genetic/metabolic data; mitochondrial/metabolic and vascular alternatives ranked lower with stated caveats). It appropriately does not overclaim: it flags that no biochemical or genetic results are available (consistent with Q3 feedback), treats the brother's symptoms cautiously, and does not infer untreated status (Q5). Management is linked to the trajectory: calcium/phosphate/PTH, formal neuropsychology, genetic testing, and prolonged EEG to characterise semiology—all proportionate and tied to the identified uncertainties. The course interpretation is correct, graded, and connected to next actions, meeting the score-5 anchor.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: All three frozen essential requirements are met by targeted, appropriately timed requests within the six turns: R1 (longitudinal caregiver history) via Q1 and Q4; R2 (objective neurological/cognitive and EEG data) via Q2 and Q4; R3 (brain imaging, including earlier imaging) via Q2, which also retrieved the age-6 CT comparison. Requests were prioritised (history first, then objective data, then discriminating extras such as family/metabolic screening in Q3 and seizure semiology in Q5), each with a prospectively allowed note explaining how the information would shape the differential. Unavailable details (milestones, metabolic results, semiology variation) were adequately requested and count as fulfilled despite simulator limits, with no invented findings. The requests are proportionate, discriminating, and avoid unnecessary gathering, meeting the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission clearly separates established findings (documented calcifications on serial CT, EEG sharp/slow waves, MMSE 12, seizure frequency) from provisional interpretations, ranks the differential by likelihood ('most consistent', 'could explain', 'supported by... though less typical'), names the specific source of uncertainty for each hypothesis (no genetic/metabolic results in the packet; no biochemical screening data; atypical imaging distribution), and identifies concrete next steps that would reduce each uncertainty (calcium/phosphate/PTH, neuropsychological testing, genetic panel/exome, prolonged EEG). It also avoids overclaiming where evidence is genuinely absent—e.g., it does not treat the healthy parents as excluding inheritance and hedges the brother's relevance. This meets the Score 5 anchor: established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions are distinguished, uncertainty sources are explained, and next steps to resolve them are stated.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.
Correct chronology with explicit temporal anchors (e.g., “on Day 3 of admission…” ) [13]
Correct, graded, and linked to management decisions

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
D5c.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

evaluation_input.source: https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2026.1865322; adapted published facts; later outcomes withheld.
evaluation_input.reference: Preserve the distinction between childhood learning difficulty, a reported relatively stable adolescent interval, adult seizure onset and family-reported further cognitive deterioration. MMSE 12 establishes a low current score but does not quantify an acquired decline from childhood. Integrate received imaging and EEG with the clinical course to form a provisional structural, vascular, metabolic or inherited-neurological differential, with appropriate seizure assessment. Do not require the undisclosed biopsy, genetic result or final label. A healthy parental history does not settle inheritance, and the brother's symptoms do not establish the same condition. Requesting more detailed baseline/serial neuropsychological evidence is appropriate even though it is unavailable. Candidate essential requests and clinical prioritisation await confirmation.

requirements.requirement: Seek caregiver-supported childhood, seizure and cognitive chronology.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Recurrent impaired consciousness with cognitive difficulty needs a longitudinal history, and the task explicitly asks whether childhood and adult findings belong to the same course.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: A collateral timeline covering early symptoms/learning, onset and recurrence of seizures, and reported adult functional change. Exact ages are not required in the question, and earlier records may substitute where caregiver recall is limited.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request objective current neurological/cognitive and seizure-assessment records.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Caregiver-reported decline and recurrent loss of awareness should be considered alongside current examination, cognitive assessment and electrophysiological evidence.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current neurological/cognitive examination plus EEG, or an equivalent specialist seizure-and-cognition assessment. No particular cognitive instrument or numerical score must be guessed.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request available brain imaging, including relevant earlier imaging if accessible.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Recurrent seizures, visual/headache episodes and cognitive difficulty raise a consequential structural question independently of any hidden genetic result.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Current CT/MRI or a clinically equivalent structural-neurological investigation request, with comparison to earlier records where available. Asking for biopsy or a specific gene is not required.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

turns.question: Could you describe the childhood developmental and learning history—when cognitive difficulties were first noticed, whether any milestones were delayed or missed, and how her educational needs evolved over time? Also, when did the recurrent episodes of impaired consciousness first begin, and how have their frequency or character changed since onset?
turns.notes: Establishing the developmental trajectory and episode timeline is essential to distinguish a static encephalopathy with superimposed seizures from a progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic process, and to frame the differential.
turns.feedback: Specific developmental milestones, any delayed/missed milestones, and educational support or accommodations are not supplied in the stored packet; do not infer normal milestones or an absence of additional educational needs. Further adult cognitive-change detail in 10.family_reported_cognition is deferred because of the two-group cap, not declared unavailable. Childhood headache/visual episodes are not reclassified as impaired-consciousness events.
turns.reply:
Learning difficulties appeared at about seven, with persistently poor primary-school performance. Between ages 15 and 21, no substantial neurological deterioration was reported.
At age 22 she had a probable focal seizure progressing to a bilateral tonic-clonic event while cycling, preceded by headache and blurred vision, with incontinence and foaming at the mouth. From 22 to 24, episodes recurred once or twice monthly.

turns.question: What are the findings on her EEG (including any epileptiform discharges, their morphology, and lateralisation) and on structural brain imaging (MRI or CT), including any cortical, subcortical, or other abnormalities noted?
turns.notes: Objective electroencephalographic and structural data are essential to characterise the seizure semiology, identify a potential structural aetiology, and narrow the differential between focal epilepsies, encephalopathies, and other causes of recurrent impaired consciousness.
turns.feedback: The selected groups provide the stored EEG morphology/regional distribution and the available childhood/adult structural-imaging descriptions. Finer EEG waveform/localisation or imaging detail beyond those stored descriptions is not supplied; it must not be invented. No directly responsive group is deferred by the two-group cap.
turns.records:
[10.eeg; presentation] The admission EEG showed sharp and slow waves in the bilateral occipital and parietal regions.
[10.imaging; presentation] At age six, CT had shown small intracranial calcifications. At the adult admission, CT showed widespread basal-ganglia and cerebellar calcifications and two cystic lesions with fluid levels. MRI showed right thalamic and parietal cysts plus diffuse periventricular/deep-white-matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement.

turns.question: Is there any family history of similar neurological symptoms, cognitive difficulties, or intracranial calcifications in relatives? Also, have any metabolic or endocrine investigations been performed—such as serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, or other biochemical screens—and if so, what were the results?
turns.notes: Family history and metabolic/endocrine data are critical to distinguish primary familial brain calcification from secondary causes (hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism) and to assess inheritance pattern.
turns.feedback: The selected family-history group supplies the documented relatives history. Relatives' brain-imaging/calcification findings are not supplied, so clinically healthy parents are not treated as negative imaging or biochemical screens. Serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and other metabolic/endocrine-screening results are not provided in any frozen requestable group. Their absence from this packet does not establish that such tests were not performed. No additional directly responsive group is deferred by the two-group cap.
turns.reply: The parents were reported to be clinically healthy and were not consanguineous. Her younger brother reported mild memory difficulty but remained functionally independent; he had not undergone the genetic testing described in the report.

turns.question: Could you describe the adult cognitive change that has been reported—what specific domains are affected (memory, attention, executive function, language), how rapidly it has progressed, and how it impacts her daily functioning? Also, on the adult neurological examination, were there any findings in the motor, cerebellar, or visual-field domains (e.g., ataxia, extrapyramidal signs, visual field defects, or papilloedema)?
turns.notes: The deferred adult cognitive-change detail and the adult examination findings (motor, cerebellar, visual) are needed to characterise the syndrome's phenotype and to distinguish among calcification-associated neurodegenerative, metabolic, and mitochondrial aetiologies.
turns.feedback: Specific attention, executive or language deficits, an objectively quantified rate of adult decline, and detailed daily-function examples are not supplied by the stored family report. The adult examination group provides only its documented motor/sensory/gait, MMSE and ophthalmological findings. A complete cerebellar or extrapyramidal assessment, formal visual fields and an explicit papilloedema finding are not separately supplied; do not expand the recorded examination into negatives for every example in the question or infer those assessments were not performed. No directly responsive group is deferred by the two-group cap.
turns.reply: The family noticed further memory and everyday cognitive difficulty in early adulthood, especially after recurrent seizures began. This is a reported change on top of longstanding learning difficulty; the report has no serial standardized cognitive assessments to quantify that change.
turns.records: [10.adult_examination; presentation] At admission, muscle strength, sensation and gait were normal, and the ophthalmological examination was unremarkable. MMSE was 12. Formal neuropsychological testing beyond MMSE was not completed.

turns.question: Regarding the recurrent episodes between ages 22 and 24: were they all similar to the first event (headache, blurred vision, then convulsion), or did some present as shorter focal events—such as visual phenomena or impaired awareness without convulsion? Also, was any antiseizure medication started, and if so, what was the response?
turns.notes: Clarifying the semiology of recurrent episodes refines seizure classification and localisation; treatment response informs management and may hint at aetiology.
turns.feedback: The frozen seizure-course group describes the first age-22 event and the recurrence frequency from 22 to 24, but does not establish that all recurrent events had the same semiology or describe shorter nonconvulsive focal events. Their occurrence or absence is therefore unknown from this packet. Any earlier antiseizure-treatment history is not supplied at this selected pre-confirmation review; subsequent treatment initiation and response remain withheld. Do not infer that she was untreated, that medication was never started, or that any treatment failed. No directly responsive stored group is deferred by the two-group cap.
